title: [Toyota Times] Akio Toyoda, the New "Chief Officer": What's Behind the Move?
summary: “Chief Officer” Akio Toyoda and President Kenta Kon discuss the background of the Toyota Philosophy and Education Group, announced by Toyota on November 5, and their hopes for its future. #TOYOTATIMES
body_markdown:
"Chief Officer" Akio Toyoda and President Kenta Kon discuss the background of the Toyota Philosophy and Education Group, announced by Toyota on November 5, and their hopes for its future.


This edition of Voice-Only Toyota Times News looks at the Toyota Philosophy and Education Group, the first organization of its kind at Toyota. On November 5, Toyota announced that it will establish the group on January 1, 2027.


According to the release, Chairman Akio Toyoda will lead the new organization as Chief Officer. Why education and why now? What does the group intend to do? We spoke with “Chief Officer” Toyoda and his “boss,” President Kenta Kon, who formally notified him of his upcoming appointment.


“I have no intention whatsoever of offering some kind of education package in the form of training,” Chief Officer Toyoda declared.


During his presidency, Akio dealt with one crisis after another, from operating losses and recalls to the Great East Japan Earthquake. Having navigated these challenges, he has much to offer those working alongside him in real-world situations rather than in formal training sessions.


This education will not be limited to Toyota. Akio says he wants to engage with the entire auto industry and, at times, with other industries and students.


The episode also features the moment President Kon formally informs Chairman Toyoda of his new appointment. (Executive Vice President Yoichi Miyazaki, who will be his other “boss,” was also present.)


“I will do everything I can to pass on my way of life.”


Read on to learn more about Chief Officer Toyoda’s new challenge and President Kon’s thoughts, in their own words.


### The “bosses,” President Kon and Executive Vice President Miyazaki


**Yuta Tomikawa**
Hello to everyone listening to Toyota Times. I’m Yuta Tomikawa. We’re recording this edition of Voice-Only Toyota Times News on November 3, Culture Day in Japan, which is also the anniversary of Toyota’s founding. On this special day, our guest, Chairman Akio Toyoda, was informed that he will serve as the first Chief Officer of the Toyota Philosophy and Education Group, a new group Toyota will establish for its future on January 1, 2027.


Thanks for joining us.


(Applause from the audience)


**Chairman Toyoda** That’s quite a look on your face.


**Tomikawa**
(Laughs) It was a bolt from the bl... I’m so stunned I can’t even say “bolt from the blue.” Akio-san, the Chairman, will serve as Chief Officer?


**Chairman Toyoda** So I’ve been told.


**Tomikawa**
Right. Since this is about the appointment, let’s have President Kenta Kon join us so the three of us can talk about it.


Is this the first education group for Toyota?


**Chairman Toyoda** Haven’t we had one before?


**Tomikawa** There hasn’t, at least as far as I could find.


**President Kon** No, there hasn’t. There may have been an Education Division, though.


**Tomikawa** Isn’t it extremely unusual for a chairman to serve as a chief officer?


**Chairman Toyoda** Yes.


**President Kon** I’d say so.


**Tomikawa** President Kon looks very nervous right now. We actually have video of Akio-san being informed of his appointment this morning. Let’s listen to how President Kon delivered the news.


(Recording of the appointment)


**President Kon**
Effective January 1, 2027, we will establish the Toyota Philosophy and Education Group. The executive team has decided to ask you, Chairman Toyoda, to serve as its first Chief Officer. This has been discussed and approved by the Executive Appointment Meeting.


I am here today on behalf of the executive team to formally ask you to take on this role. We hope you will accept.


**Chairman Toyoda** I accept.


**President Kon**
Chairman, wherever you are is where Toyota’s most important work begins. Whether in production and sales, motorsports, or now education, I believe you have always been at the heart of what matters most to Toyota. We have left you to fight alone for a long time, but with this appointment, the executive team wants to ask you aloud to let us fight alongside you.


We look forward to working with you.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Thank you. I will do everything I can to pass on my way of life.


That said, rather than creating and running training programs, I want to focus on developing people through work.


**All** (Laughter)


**Executive Vice President Miyazaki** I never sweat this much.


(End of recording)


**Tomikawa** That was just a short clip, with President Kon reading out the appointment and Executive Vice President Miyazaki sitting beside him. They were both incredibly nervous, Akio-san.


**Chairman Toyoda**
At first, they said they’d come to the Chairman’s office at headquarters to inform me, so I said, “That’s not right.” “Isn’t the person receiving the appointment supposed to go to you?”


**Tomikawa**
So you went to see President Kon.


**Chairman Toyoda**
That’s right. They had it backwards at first, so I said, “No, I’ll come to you.” I also told them, “Record it while you’re at it.”


I did it all properly. I knocked on the door to the President’s office, stood up straight, and bowed before entering. When I heard “Come in,” I went in and received the appointment.


They were so nervous. A lot of appointments went out about a week ago, didn’t they?


**President Kon**
Yes, for many people.


**Chairman Toyoda**
I’d heard about it and said, “I still haven’t received an appointment.” Then today, since I was coming to headquarters, they said, “Shall we do it now?” It felt like an afterthought.


**President Kon**
That’s not true at all.


**Tomikawa**
Since he’d be here for this recording anyway?


**President Kon**
No. It was my most important job today.


**Tomikawa**
So were you actually nervous?


**President Kon**
Yes, of course I was, and Executive Vice President Miyazaki, who will be the Chairman’s direct boss, was probably even more nervous.


**Tomikawa**
I see, so Miyazaki-san will be Akio-san’s boss.


**Chairman Toyoda**
That’s right.


They say it takes a boss three years to figure out a subordinate, but a subordinate can figure out a boss in three days.


I’ve known Executive Vice President Miyazaki for many years, but as chairman, it’s hard to tell what someone is really like. So I thought I’d become his subordinate and figure him out in three days.


**Tomikawa**
Could we pass the mic to Miyazaki? Miyazaki-san, how do you feel about becoming his direct boss?


**Executive Vice President Miyazaki**
I don’t think I’ve ever had such a difficult subordinate.


Like Nakajima-san, I always gather my team at the start of the year and tell them, “Here’s how we’re going to approach the year.” I’m already wondering what I’m going to say.


**Tomikawa**
When you gather your team, Akio-san will be there.


**Executive Vice President Miyazaki**
Normally, I’d also set the date and time around my own schedule. I’m not sure what to do this time.


**Tomikawa**
It would be strange to ask a subordinate when he's available, wouldn't it?


**Chairman Toyoda**
That would be strange.


**Executive Vice President Miyazaki**
Well, I’ll have my secretary work something out... Looks like I’ll have plenty of challenges like that next year.


### Carrying the Toyota name


**Tomikawa**
Thank you. It sounds like Miyazaki-san has a stressful New Year ahead.


The Toyota Philosophy and Education Group, which Akio-san will lead, currently has three pillars that define its purpose.


First, education that goes beyond conventional training to pass on Toyota’s history, philosophy, and values.
Second, Toyota Sports, which fosters a commitment to giving your all for others and for the team through sports.
Third, Toyota’s technical training schools, among them Toyota Technical Skills Academy, which pass on manufacturing skills and the Toyota mindset to the next generation.


Those are the three current pillars. President Kon, I see it covers both sports and Toyota Technical Skills Academy.


**President Kon**
Yes. When I was secretary to then-President Toyoda in 2010 and 2011, the company was going through a very difficult time. Many members of our sports teams are here today, but there were discussions within the company about whether to keep the sports teams back then.


The Chairman never said anything in response. Instead, every weekend, he was at softball one day, basketball the next, then rugby, then baseball, cheering them on week after week, not from the executive seats but alongside regular employees.


Seeing the Chairman's dedication, I remember him saying, “Our athletes wear the Toyota name on their chests and carry it on their backs, just like I do.”


It made me realize that what we share with one another through the Toyota name is another important lesson. Personally, I’m very happy that sports and skills training are part of what we’re calling education.


**Tomikawa**
I see. So is it meant to be a place that develops people like Akio-san, who carry the Toyota name and act for the sake of others?


**President Kon** Thank you. Yes, exactly.


**Tomikawa**
Akio-san, what were your thoughts when you accepted the role?


**Chairman Toyoda**
Even though it has “Education” in its name, I have no intention whatsoever of offering some kind of education package in the form of training.


Rather than education for its own sake, I want people to see how I deal with others and how I get my message across in the course of real work. I’ve tried different approaches over the years, including Akio Juku and various projects.


Of everything I’ve experienced in my years at the company, what helped me most was what I learned through hands-on experience, doing real work. That’s what truly became part of who I am.


Rather than setting out a fixed program for the group, I want to use my role as Chief Officer to get involved in different areas of work, giving people a chance to see how I approach and think about things.


I probably won’t offer solutions, but I’ll think through problems with them and fight alongside them as we work out what to do.


### Showing a way of life


**Chairman Toyoda**
Looking back on my life at Toyota, I feel like I’ve been on a battlefield the whole time.


I started out constantly hearing “You can’t do it.” When I became president, nobody wanted me there, and I got the sense they wanted me to take responsibility for the losses and resign.


Through all that, I dealt with the losses, got through the quality issues that came right after, and then faced the Great East Japan Earthquake, which devastated much of Japan, as the person responsible for making decisions.


I believe that series of experiences is why I’m still in this position today.


I went through one crisis after another, and I think what I did and said in those moments will come through naturally. Now I’d like to share that with everyone through our work together.


I’m 70, so I won’t be in a position to work alongside all of you at the company for much longer. My time is very limited.


The question is how much of my way of life I can show in the time I have left.


People often talk about “Morizo’s principles” or “Akio’s principles,” and there are times I wonder if that’s quite right. I’m still a living example, after all, so it’s a little different from compiling the sayings of someone who has passed away. Since I’m a living example, I think my role as Chief Officer is to give people chances to work on projects with me and see how I do things.


**Tomikawa** I see.


**Chairman Toyoda**
That makes it real rather than some artificial kind of on-the-job training. It’s in real work that people can develop their individuality.


I was something of a minority within the company myself. People were quick to say, “He’s from the founding family” or “He’s a spoiled rich kid,” and I clashed with the majority.


Even so, I had allies, and as I thought things through, made my own decisions, and took action, I gradually built a track record that changed the way people saw me.


Before I knew it, more and more people had joined me to help build the future together.


I very much want to share those experiences, and I believe real work and real company life offer endless material for doing so.


I don’t think the Toyota Philosophy and Education Group should be about saying, “We’re holding a lecture in a classroom, so please attend.”


Education also isn’t something to keep inside the company, and since Toyota makes cars, a consumer product, I think we need to engage with the public and other industries.


For example, I recently visited the National Institute of Technology, Kumamoto College, in the area hit by the earthquake.


**Tomikawa**
The Yatsushiro Campus.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Through my connection with Takeshi Okada, I also held Akio Juku at FC Imabari High School Satoyama, and I’m getting more chances to do things with people of high school age.


High school is a time of real uncertainty, when students wonder what kind of adult they’ll become and whether what they’ve done so far has been right. I can share in that uncertainty with them. I’ve started to think I may be well suited to that.


That’s why I think we can do all kinds of things through contact with the wider world, beyond education that stays in-house.


### Education versus training


**Tomikawa**
So the group isn’t just an internal matter, since it involves the entire industry and can provide hands-on education in the genba. I imagine that will open up great opportunities, which makes it something entirely different from training.


**Chairman Toyoda**
I’m not dismissing training, but to me, education means thinking, struggling, and forging a path on your own, while training is about refining the manual and telling people to just follow it. It makes me feel like, “Don’t treat people like fools.”


Everyone is different, and I believe it’s a human privilege to struggle and fail as we move forward. So when I hear “Just do what the manual says”...


But I’ve rarely seen anyone actually come out on top just by following instructions.


People who keep going despite the struggles, mistakes, and failures are far more compelling, and I think there are many people with that kind of potential in the auto industry, and even more so in the Toyota Group. I hope we can also find people like that and bring out their potential.


In short, I want to create more opportunities for such people.


**Tomikawa**
OK.


**Chairman Toyoda**
But I’d tell them, “You have to lay your own tracks.” That’s what it comes down to.


**Tomikawa**
I see.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Right now, I feel that those opportunities are limited. The ones that do exist are also very uniform.


When Toyota first got into cars, it started with imitation. Toyota began by bringing in foreign cars, taking them apart completely, and trying to build the same thing. Imitation then turned into improvement, which gave rise to the philosophy of kaizen.


Making high-quality products required people to work in a consistent way. That is still necessary, but now that we’ve reached the stage where innovation is expected of us, we also need diversity. I think we also need to value individuality a little more and engage with people one by one rather than treating everyone the same.


### Human respect


**Chairman Toyoda**
Two weeks ago, I met Brunello Cucinelli*.
*Founder of the fashion brand Brunello Cucinelli and advocate of “humanistic capitalism,” which values the dignity of artisans.


Brunello Cucinelli is an Italian designer who, having watched his father go unrewarded as a factory worker, has given back to his home village in many ways while building his fashion business.


He told me, “I want working people, especially those who make things, to be given more dignity. Toyota is the only company doing that.” “Toyota has tremendous respect for its employees who make things,” he said.


He also said, “You may not see it because you live in that world, but in society at large, and especially around the world, the dignity of making things for a living has been disappearing. I’d like you to spread that respect around the world.”


**Tomikawa**
I see.


**Chairman Toyoda**
I can’t judge that myself, but this may be one of the things Toyota has done for years.


It’s human respect, as typified by jidoka, or automation with a human touch. As Chief Officer, I hope to explore human respect and my belief that roles matter more than titles by working with different people. If that helps us see what lies ahead, I feel I can give something back to Toyota for creating this group.


The vision and mission haven’t been clearly decided yet, but through what I do and say...


I’m not the only one in the group, am I? There are other members, right?


**President Kon** Yes.


**Chairman Toyoda**
You’re not going to leave me all on my own, are you?


**President Kon**
No, of course not.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Then I’m sure those people will give it some thought.


**Tomikawa**
There’ll be a working team, too?


**President Kon**
Yes.


**Chairman Toyoda**
They say that, but sometimes they leave me to do it alone.


**Tomikawa**
We have it on record now.


**Chairman Toyoda** Right.


**President Kon**
Yes, it’ll be fine.


### Toyota’s strength


**Tomikawa**
The world sees Toyota as a company that respects people who make things because Akio-san has fought for so long to bring Toyota back to its roots. Is the idea to develop more people within Toyota like Akio-san, who is creating opportunities for things like that right now?


**President Kon**
Yes. As the Chairman just said, the formal term would be “respect for human dignity,” but he puts it as “Don’t treat people like fools.”


**Tomikawa**
That’s a blunt way to put it.


**President Kon**
That is what the Chairman has been doing all along, and I hope we can fight alongside him to keep this going.


**Chairman Toyoda**
This may sound like criticism, but until now, Toyota has been trying to develop supermen.


**Tomikawa**
Elite education.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Maybe not elite, but it means having one person able to do anything and everything.


While that would be great someday, I’m no superman. I can’t do anything on my own. That’s why I have allies. I’m surrounded by people more capable than I am.


All I do is bring their strengths together to create something even better. I’m certainly not trying to create supermen.


When people work together and inspire one another, one plus one can become three or four instead of two. That’s the power of shared purpose. I think that’s where our sports teams are strong.


Individual ability matters too. I want people to hone their own abilities first.


A baseball team has nine players on the field, but there are substitutes too, making perhaps 15 to 18 players on the roster for the game. Some don’t even make the bench. My point is that they’re all teammates. They all practice together.


I think that combined strength is what Toyota is all about.


It isn’t only the nine on the field who are fighting. The same goes for a company.


**Tomikawa**
A group of individuals who are each experts in their field is stronger than one superman.


**Chairman Toyoda**
They won’t win if everyone moves the same way, either.


**Tomikawa**
Everyone has a role.


**Chairman Toyoda**
All team members have incredibly strong personalities.


People often call me a beast tamer, and I’m fine with having beasts. We do need to develop other tamers, though, because I won’t be around forever.


We don’t want everyone turning into a well-behaved pedigree dog. (pointing toward Executive Vice President Hiroki Nakajima) We need mad dogs too.


**Tomikawa**
You mean Nakajima-san.


**Chairman Toyoda**
No, I wasn’t pointing at him.


**Tomikawa**
He just happened to be where your finger was.


**Chairman Toyoda**
He just happened to be there.


**All**
(Laughter)


**Executive Vice President Nakajima**
Woof!


**Tomikawa**
From his face, you’d expect a scarier bark, but he’s kind at heart.


### Cherishing the present


**Tomikawa**
I’d also like to ask why this group is being created now. This is said to be a once-in-a-century transformation, and with U.S. tariffs and the situation in the Middle East, there’s no telling what lies ahead. Does Toyota need this group now in order to weather such difficult times?


**Chairman Toyoda**
No. I’ve been appointed now, so I think it’s important to make the most of this moment. However strongly I feel about something, I think the right time to act is when the people around me feel the same and ask me to do it.


**Tomikawa**
I see.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Wanting to do something isn’t enough to move the world. That’s why people talk about the time being ripe. I think that’s why it’s happening now.


**Tomikawa**
So the executive team asked you because they felt it was necessary, not because you told them to work on education.


**Chairman Toyoda**
I told them to do it two or three years ago, but I don’t think they should just say “Yes, sir” and do it because I told them to. Even if I am a... you-know-what.


**Tomikawa**
A you-know-what. (laughs)


**Chairman Toyoda** Yes. (laughs)


**Tomikawa**
A dictator.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Exactly... Wait, this is radio, isn’t it?


**Tomikawa**
It is.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Then there’s no problem with me calling myself a dictator. I do think a dictator like this is fine, though.


**Tomikawa**
Yes, there’s a purpose behind it. Some things can’t get done any other way. President Kon, you asked him to be Chief Officer only because all of you discussed it and felt it was necessary now, right?


**President Kon**
Right. It was the consensus of the executive team, and I made the request on their behalf.


**Chairman Toyoda**
He was so nervous when he told me about the appointment.


**Tomikawa**
He was.


**President Kon**
I had a lot on my mind, such as which of us should sit in the seat of honor.


**Tomikawa**
This is a simple question, Akio-san, but you’re busy enough as it is. Won’t this make you even busier?


**Chairman Toyoda**
That’s exactly why I think I can educate people through the work I already do.


Rather than starting something new because it’s an education group, I’ll draw on the many things I’m already involved in, such as the groundwork I do ahead of the executive team. In that work, I might get a little support by saying, “This counts as education, so the education group can help out.” If that becomes an opportunity for people to learn, I think that’s good enough.


**Tomikawa** I see.


### Keep an eye on Toyota’s products, its people, and Chief Officer Akio Toyoda!


**Tomikawa** Lastly, I’m sure many employees are listening to this broadcast, along with Toyota Times listeners. What about Toyota would you like people to keep an eye on going forward?


**Chairman Toyoda**
What to keep an eye on at Toyota? I’d say the way we transform ourselves.


We’ll remain grateful and humble even when we’re called number one in the world, but work with the conviction that if our company doesn’t do its best, Japan and the countries that have been good to us will suffer. That is the way of life I hope people will see in Toyota, whether they support us, criticize us, or quietly root for us.


Toyota also expresses itself through its products, which are the sum of what our 400,000 employees around the world do and say. It all comes down to how people see those products.


The products we keep putting out are the clearest way for us to communicate with the world. I’d love for people to pay attention to both the products and the people who make them.


**Tomikawa** I hope everyone will keep an eye on Toyota’s products, its people, and Chief Officer Akio Toyoda.


**Chairman Toyoda**


I can see Powertrain Company President Takashi Uehara over there, so let me add that “products” covers engines too. He gave me a look that said, “You mean cars.”


**Tomikawa**
They’re trying a lot of new things with engines right now, too.


Let’s wrap up this broadcast here before we dig ourselves into a hole. Akio-san, President Kon, thank you very much.


**Chairman Toyoda**
Thank you.


**President Kon**
Thank you.
